subject: Trouble adding mean categorical psi covariate to newdata for predict function

messages.author: eac7a87541688ade
messages.subject: Trouble adding mean categorical psi covariate to newdata for predict function
parts:
Hi all,

I am a new user of unmarked, so I apologise if this is an obvious fix. I've had a good sift through of old topics but cannot find a solution.

I've fit a full with continous and categorical covs of both p and psi = p (effort + camtype + period) psi (elevation + lctype) and using this, I wish to predict occupancy estimates for elevation across averaged values of the other covs. My trouble starts when I include the categorical psi covariate 'lctype'. In the Carly Scott thread ("Predict() with categorical survey-level covariate in top models") the advice was to specify one level of the factors - when I do this, it generates predictions of that specific lctype (landcover type) successfully in a normal looking plot, but when I change this to another lctype factor level, the prediction changes and its clear that its predicting for elevation within that factor level. 

My question is: how do I format the newdata so that I am predicting across averaged values of the lctype psi cov?

Here is what I've got so far:

mod2 <- occu(formula = ~effort + camtype + period
             ~  elevation + lctype,
             data = umf)

newdata <- data.frame(elevation=seq(500, 2250, length=315),
                      effort = 0, 
                      period = c('period1',
                                  'period2',
                                  'period3'),
                       camtype = c('Acorn',
                                   'Browning',
                                   'Reconyx'),
                      lctype =c('Alpineherbfield',
                                'Beechforest',
                                'Matagourigrassland',
                                'Lowproducingpasture',
                                'Rock',
                                'Subalpineshrub',
                                'Talltussockgrassland'))

If I try something like 

newdata$lctype <- factor(lctype, levels = c('Alpineherbfield', '.......)

messages.author: 4f80e1927b0757cb
messages.subject: Re: Trouble adding mean categorical psi covariate to newdata for predict function
parts:
Hi Nicholas,

There's no straightforward way to do what you are asking in unmarked. If you provide multiple factor levels in the newdata as you have done in your example, you will get one predicted value for each of these factor levels. These predictions will have the same value for x (elevation) but different values of y, which leads to the ugly plot you are seeing. 

Usually for a plot like the one you are making, focused on one continuous covariate, I would just use the baseline/reference levels of each categorical covariate, or plot multiple lines on each plot with each line corresponding to a different factor level. It doesn't really make sense to me conceptually to try to get the "mean" of a categorical variable. If you have elevation measurements of 0 and 100, the mean=50 is generally a possible observed value in the dataset. But "averaging" across land covers is creating a new "category" that doesn't exist in reality.

If you really want this I suppose you could get predicted values for your range of elevations at each individual land cover level, one at a time, and then calculate an average value across all land covers for each elevation value in your sequence.

Ken

messages.author: 7ad0c15c3067da73
messages.subject: Re: Trouble adding mean categorical psi covariate to newdata for predict function
parts:
Hi Nick, 

Not exactly an answer to the question you're asking, but I think this might help. If you're interested in seeing the effect of elevation on PSI in the different land cover types you could visualize that by modifying how you're plotting the predicted dataframe (of course this will be the same slope without an interaction term, but as a place to start) . Try plotting with ggplot and use facet_wrap(~lctype). That will give you 7 different panels, with PSI on the y axis, and elevation of the x. If you're not familiar with ggplot that code might look something like this for you:

#make your predicted dataframe
pred_data<-predict(mod2, type="state", newdata=newdata, appendData=TRUE)


#plot it
ggplot(pred_data , aes(elevation,Predicted))+
geom_line()+
geom_ribbon(aes(ymin =lower, ymax = upper), alpha = 0.3)+
ylab(expression(italic(psi)))+
xlab(elevation)+
facet_wrap(~lctype)

Hope this helps. 
Kevin
